key_insight: A machine-learning pipeline can infer family relationships from EHR data with high precision by combining record linkage, feature engineering, and iterative model refinement.
clinical_relevance: Accurate family-relationship inference could improve patient-centered research and care coordination, but it is best suited to secondary data uses rather than direct clinical decision-making.
method: Trained Random Forest classifiers for five relationship types: mother-child, father-child, sibling-sibling, twin-twin, and partner-partner.
Used Indiana EHR and natality data, with verified natality links as the gold standard and negative pairs generated through blocking and similarity filtering.
Refined models in four stages: initial training, multicollinearity reduction, feature engineering, and training-data restriction to pairs with shared contact features.
evidence_signal: Across large Indiana datasets, the models achieved precision of 0.92-1.00, recall of 0.97-1.00, and F1 scores of 0.94-1.00, with high-confidence predictions capturing 77-99% of true positives.
watch_item: A substantial share of verified relationships had no shared contact information in the EHR and were structurally undetectable, so real-world performance may depend heavily on data completeness and linkage quality.
paper_title: Identifying Family Relationships from Electronic Health Records: A Machine Learning Approach
